events.content:
View transitions are in place and verified — the build compiles with type-checking clean, and both pages render correctly at runtime.

**How it works.** This is Next.js 16.4 canary, where React's `<ViewTransition>` component is available directly from `'react'` in the vendored canary channel — the old `experimental.viewTransition` config flag no longer exists (I confirmed it's gone from the config schema), so no `next.config.ts` change was needed.

**What I changed:**

- **Shared element morph** — The grid thumbnail (`app/ProductGrid.tsx`) and the detail hero (`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`) are each wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`} share="product-image-morph">`. Because the names match across pages, React pairs them during navigation and the browser morphs position and size between the thumbnail and the large image — in both directions. The CSS only tunes the built-in morph's duration and easing.

- **Directional page slides** — Each page's root is wrapped in a `<ViewTransition>` with `enter`/`exit` classes based on where the page "lives": home enters from and exits to the left, detail enters from and exits to the right. Navigating grid → detail slides everything left; going back (link or browser back button) slides everything right — correct directionality with no navigation-direction tracking needed.

- **Suspense reveals** — The `<Suspense>` boundaries on both pages are wrapped in `<ViewTransition default="cross-fade">`, so when React reveals content in place of the skeleton it runs a 250ms cross-fade (with a size morph if the layout shifts) instead of popping.

- **Reduced motion** — A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block in `app/globals.css` sets `animation: none !important` on all four view-transition pseudo-elements (`group`, `image-pair`, `old`, `new`), which makes every transition resolve as an instant swap. It also stops the skeleton pulse animation.

- **Supporting changes** — Added `react-canary.d.ts` with `/// <reference types="react/canary" />` so TypeScript picks up the `ViewTransition` declarations from `@types/react`, and wrapped the detail page in `<main>` (it was a bare `<div>`) so both pages share the same centered container and the slides look consistent.

One note: `<ViewTransition>` is still an experimental React API surface (stable export name, canary channel), and the View Transitions API itself requires a Chromium-based browser or Safari 18+ — in Firefox, navigation simply happens without animation, which is a graceful fallback.
